This tour simultaneously glides through imagery from NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes of the Cat’s Head Nebula. The dust filament broadly remains the same in shape across the different wavelengths of light, but each view contains different details.
Hubble’s visible-light image shows the “cat” as an opaque, dark brown pillar with a glowing red eye—most likely a young star embedded in the dust.
Webb’s infrared observations reveal some of the cat’s structure and faint background filaments of dust to its left. In near-infrared light, Webb pierces through some of the dust to reveal many stars and even background galaxies. In mid-infrared light, the telescope images the emission from warm dust and carbon-based molecules excited by starlight.
Science Release Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula Lurks Within Sight of NASA’s Hubble, Webb Read the release

Image: Cat's Head Nebula (Hubble WFC3 Image)
NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope shows an opaque dust pillar edged by a luminous rim of gas. Surrounding blue regions include emission from ionized gas and scattered starlight. The cat’s glowing red eye may indicate a young star embedded in the dust.
Image: Cat's Head Nebula (Webb NIRCam Image)
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope’s near-infrared view reveals detailed structures in the pillar and many stars, as well as some background galaxies. The glowing yellow eye may be a young star embedded in dust.
Image: Cat's Head Nebula (Webb MIRI Image)
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope’s mid-infrared view reveals intricate structures within the nebula, traced by the emission from warm dust and carbon-based molecules excited by starlight.
Video: Exploring the Cat's Head Nebula
This visualization explores imagery from NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a relatively small, dusty filament containing forming stars located within the massive Carina Nebula.
